claims.text: The steels' corrosion resistance is caused by formation of a continuous, chromium-enriched passive oxide layer.
The chromium-enriched passive oxide layer self-heals after damage.
The passive oxide layer prevents aggressive species from reaching the metal substrate.
The passive film is composed primarily of chromium oxide.
Passive-film continuity, thickness, and adherence mediate corrosion resistance.
Under oxidizing conditions, chromium in the steel migrates to the surface.
Surface chromium oxidizes to form a thin, adherent chromium oxide layer.
The chromium oxide layer acts as a barrier that reduces further oxidation and metal dissolution.
Steels with higher chromium levels will develop a more uniform passive film than steels with lower chromium levels.
Steels with higher chromium levels will develop a thicker chromium oxide passive film than steels with lower chromium levels.
Higher-chromium steels will exhibit significantly lower corrosion rates than lower-chromium steels under identical test conditions.
Steels with deliberately compromised oxide layers will exhibit higher corrosion rates than high-chromium steels with intact films under identical conditions.
The proposed mechanism should operate in typical corrosive chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments.
Extreme mechanical abrasion may invalidate the proposed passive-film mechanism.
Entirely non-oxidizing conditions may invalidate the proposed passive-film mechanism.
High- and low-chromium or film-compromised samples should be exposed to the same chloride-rich acidic environment at elevated temperature and controlled oxygen level.
Passive-film composition, thickness, and integrity should be measured and correlated with corrosion rate.

Comparable film characteristics and corrosion rates in low-chromium or film-compromised samples and high-chromium samples would falsify chromium-driven passive-film formation as the primary resistance mechanism.
